stage_state.summary_md:
## Principle 1: Shared Company Culture and Values

### Depth: Communicating Across Levels

Designing with data aims to reduce reliance on “gut” decision-making, thereby disrupting hierarchical structures where top-down, hunch-based choices dominate. A data-literate environment encourages well-formulated questions, invites challenge, and accepts the possibility of being wrong. Data gathered through diverse methods—A/B testing, ethnographic field research, prototype deployments, surveys, lab studies, usability research—provides a less risky foundation than individual executives’ gut feelings.

A 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield, “Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO,” argued that data resolves conflicts without relying on rank or company politics. John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, illustrated how data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation. Patty McCord, Netflix’s Chief Talent Officer for over 12 years, emphasized that a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for customers gives more people a voice in product development.

At Netflix, the practice of leveraging data was universally accepted, starting with CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt but embraced by all levels. Patty McCord noted that while at some companies the CEO might dictate decisions, at Netflix it was different: even executives could get caught up in thinking they knew the answer. A/B testing mitigated top-down problem-solving because everyone could learn from experimentation. When Reed Hastings had a strong product idea, he submitted it to the same rigorous A/B testing as everyone else. On rare occasions, he might dictate the exact way an idea would work, but only on “his test cell”—the experimental group he backed. That cell would be tested against others proposed by the product team. If it didn’t win, it didn’t launch. Upper management holding themselves accountable to the same process reinforced subjecting ideas to grounded review through experimentation and treating “failure” as a positive outcome.

Shifting to a data-aware framework requires examining how product and design decisions have been made historically. If decisions were largely in the hands of one or two individuals, those people must understand and recognize the value of bringing user/customer data into the process, because their individual weight will be diminished—as will the weight of any single opinion. Designers and product developers must also ask themselves whether they are comfortable with data changing the weight of their own opinions.
